question:
Patient note:
A 36-year-old man who received a deceased-donor renal transplant nine years ago for biopsy-proven focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and who continues to take twice-daily tacrolimus with low-dose mycophenolate was brought to the hospital by ground emergency medical services after waking at dawn with a tightening sensation in the chest, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea that forced him to sit upright on the edge of the bed; his spouse reported no recent changes in antirejection therapy, no missed doses, and no sick household contacts, though he had spent the previous weekend volunteering at a community animal shelter where several kittens were noted to have respiratory infections. The home blood-pressure cuff the couple keeps for tacrolimus monitoring showed numbers in the low 120s systolic, and a personal thermometer read 100 °F; because the patient felt “foggy” and was breathing faster than normal, an ambulance was summoned. Paramedics found him sitting forward, speaking in full sentences but pausing for breath; oxygen saturation on room air was 84 %, so a clear facemask connected to the portable blender was adjusted to deliver 40 % oxygen. En route he received no intravenous fluids, corticosteroids, bronchodilators, antibiotics, vasopressors, antipyretics, or analgesics, and the only intervention other than the mask was placement of a single 18-gauge antecubital catheter left capped. Transport time from front door to hospital bay was eleven minutes. On stretcher roll-in to the medical intensive care pod—and before any hospital therapy could be initiated—the clerk simultaneously documented and confirmed with a second cuff a blood pressure of 118/70 mm Hg, telemetry displayed a regular pulse of 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate counted over a full minute was 22 breaths, and an oral temperature on a digital probe registered 100.0 °F. The patient was awake, answered questions appropriately, obeyed commands, and had equal grip strength, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 without sedation or intoxicants on board. Skin was warm, lightly diaphoretic, and well perfused with capillary refill under two seconds; sclerae were anicteric, and oral mucosa moist. No jugular venous distention was seen at 30 degrees. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses were 2+ throughout. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with scattered fine inspiratory crackles over the mid-zones yet without wheeze; percussion was resonant, and tactile fremitus was symmetric. The abdomen was soft and nondistended; a well-healed right iliac fossa transplant scar was noted, and there was no costovertebral angle tenderness. No peripheral edema or clubbing was present, and neurological screening found intact cranial nerves, normal coordination, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Eight minutes after bay arrival, while he remained on the same 40 % oxygen source and before any medications or fluids were started, a right radial arterial puncture yielded bright red blood with immediate analysis showing pH 7.42, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 56 mm Hg; an end-tidal capnography trace was 35 mm Hg, correlating with the arterial value. A point-of-care metabolic panel drawn from the arterial sample reported sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 94 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 18 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL—consistent with his baseline values recorded at last nephrology follow-up. Rapid complete blood count returned a white cell count of 11 600 cells/mm³ with 72 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 41 %, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, and platelets 226 000 /µL. Venous lactate on the same stick measured 1.6 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiography performed before any antimicrobial, diuretic, or corticosteroid therapy showed patchy bilateral interstitial opacities more pronounced in the perihilar regions without pleural effusion or cardiomegaly; point-of-care lung ultrasound corroborated diffuse B-lines but no consolidation. Focused cardiac echo demonstrated a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava that collapsed approximately 50 % with inspiration, arguing against overt volume overload. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained concurrently revealed normal sinus rhythm at 92 beats per minute, PR 150 ms, QRS 86 ms, QTc 410 ms, and no ischemic changes. A bladder scan estimated 120 mL, and the straight catheter placed for output monitoring drained 55 mL of clear yellow urine over the first fifteen minutes in the unit. Importantly, from front-door contact through completion of initial diagnostics—a span of roughly forty minutes—the patient had not received intravenous crystalloid, antibiotics, bronchodilators, antipyretics, vasopressors, or supplemental steroids; the only intervention in place remained the facemask delivering 40 % inspired oxygen. Consequently, the contemporaneous physiologic and laboratory values of temperature 100.0 °F, systolic pressure 118 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 70 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 per minute, arterial pH 7.42, serum sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, hematocrit 41 %, white-cell count 11 600 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 40 %, and arterial oxygen tension 56 mm Hg represent an accurate snapshot of his uncorrected presentation for suspected opportunistic pulmonary infection in the setting of long-term immunosuppression, necessitating admission for close hemodynamic and respiratory monitoring in the intensive care environment.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. Using the available ICU admission values:
- Temperature 100.0 °F (37.8 °C) → 0; mean arterial pressure (118 + 2 × 70)/3 = 86 mm Hg → 0; heart rate 94/min → 0; respiratory rate 22/min → 0.
- Oxygenation: FiO₂ 0.40 is below 0.50, so use PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 56 mm Hg falls in the 55–60 range → 3.
- Arterial pH 7.42 → 0; sodium 138 mmol/L → 0; potassium 4.0 mmol/L → 0; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → 0.
- Hematocrit 41% → 0; WBC 11.6 × 10³/mm³ → 0; neurologic points = 15 − GCS 15 = 0.
Acute physiology subtotal = 3. Age 36 (<45) → 0. Chronic transplant immunosuppression qualifies for 5 chronic health points on this nonsurgical admission.
Total = 3 + 0 + 5 = 8.
Final answer: 8
